context: validation-led, smaller & faster than a hospital · clinical HVAC and limited medical gas gate handover

brief.intro: New to this project type? A clinic or primary healthcare centre is a much smaller, faster relative of a hospital — mostly consulting and treatment rooms rather than operating theatres — but it shares a hospital's core discipline: the mechanical and electrical systems have to be fit for clinical use and formally validated before any patient can be seen, not just functionally tested like an office fit-out. Infection-control HVAC (filtered, often single-pass air to treatment rooms), a limited medical-gas supply (oxygen and vacuum outlets rather than a full hospital manifold system) and a shielded room for minor imaging (X-ray) are the specialist scope that drives the back end of the programme, even though the building itself is simple and low-rise. Because the scope is smaller, the programme runs faster than a hospital's — but the validation-and-inspection sequence at the end, commissioning then regulatory sign-off then clinical handover, is the same discipline in miniature, and it is still the real finish line, not the last piece of joinery.

glossary.plain: oxygen and vacuum outlets to treatment rooms, fed from a compact cylinder manifold rather than a full hospital bulk plant.
filtered, often single-pass air to treatment rooms that limits cross-contamination between patients.
a lead-lined room built for a minor X-ray or imaging unit.
a smaller-scale backup supply — generator or UPS — keeping critical clinical loads and refrigeration (vaccines, medicines) running through a mains failure.
a formal sign-off and walkthrough with clinical staff before patients are seen, distinct from ordinary construction completion.
the basic clinical unit of a primary-care building, each with its own power, data and, where needed, limited medical-gas outlets.

must_get_right: Infection-control HVAC and the limited medical-gas supply need formal validation and certification, not just a functional test, before any clinical occupancy.
Where an imaging room is included, coordinate its lead-lined shielding with the structure early — retrofitting shielding afterwards is expensive and disruptive.
Essential power for clinical refrigeration (vaccines, medicines) and life-safety loads must be proven with a mains-fail test, sized to this building's much smaller scale than a hospital.
Keep the validation → regulatory inspection → clinical handover sequence on the schedule as named milestones; it is faster than a hospital's but not optional.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual and regulatory-inspection milestones.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and shell run a standard 6-day week; MEP fit-out and specialist-room works may move to extended hours to protect the programme; commissioning and clinical validation run against the availability of the health-authority inspector rather than a fixed calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structural weather-tightness → MEP first/second fix → imaging-room shielding and infection-control HVAC fit-out → essential power and limited medical-gas installation & certification → integrated systems test → health-authority inspection → clinical handover. The building shell is rarely the constraint; the specialist-system validation and certification chain owns the back end.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and room-data sheets are frozen per clinical room before rough-in; authority approvals are obtained per phase gate; a single mobilisation; the site is a new-build or a vacant renovation with no live clinical operations to work around.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Clinics are often built on small infill or urban sites with limited laydown and delivery access. Specialist medical-gas and infection-control commissioning technicians are scarce and shared across several projects, and are a resource constraint late in the programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: medical-gas re-certification loops, health-authority inspection scheduling delays outside the contractor's control, and owner-furnished imaging-equipment delivery slippage. Schedule contingency is held immediately before the integrated systems test and before the health-authority inspection, rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
